strengths: Addresses an important provenance problem with a clear, modular framework that connects user-specific watermark assignment, detection, and attribution.

Experiments cover three image sources and multiple watermarking methods, reporting strong accuracy on unmodified images. Including worst-user statistics, common post-processing, and an exploratory text extension is useful.

A-BSTA improves watermark separation and worst-user attribution over the included Random and NRG baselines. The manuscript provides pseudocode and explicitly acknowledges dependence on the underlying watermark’s robustness.
weaknesses: The novelty and baseline positioning are insufficient. User-specific watermarks and nearest-codeword attribution closely resemble classical digital fingerprinting and error-correcting codes; Theorem 4 recovers the usual half-minimum-distance decoding condition. A standard extended binary BCH code provides 262,144 length-64 codewords with minimum distance 22, giving maximum pairwise agreement of 0.65625, compared with A-BSTA’s 0.734 for 100,000 users in Table 7. This does not establish better empirical attribution, but makes a coding-based baseline essential.

The false-detection guarantee is not established for the proposed selection procedure. Theorem 3 assumes independently selected watermarks, whereas A-BSTA explicitly selects each watermark based on previous assignments. Moreover, Appendix H factors joint matching events involving the same decoded watermark without establishing their independence for a fixed deployed codebook. Section 7.3 nevertheless applies this bound. The analysis must distinguish guarantees averaged over random codebook selection from guarantees for a particular selected codebook.

The theoretical-to-empirical connection is inadequately validated. Definition 3 assumes independent, identically distributed bit errors, and Definition 4 assumes independent decoded bits with a bound on every bit’s bias. Estimating average accuracy on the evaluation images does not verify these assumptions or quantify estimation uncertainty; Figure 13 also shows substantial bitwise heterogeneity. Additionally, the statement that detection implies attribution does not follow merely from similar lower bounds on their probabilities.

The evidence does not establish sufficiently low false-positive rates or the headline deployment scale. Only 1,000 negative images are evaluated; even zero observed errors gives an approximately 0.3% one-sided 95% upper confidence bound. The 100-million-user result is an extrapolation using assumed parameters, and Table 5 reports a 6% FDR upper bound, which does not substantiate near-zero false detection at that scale. Attribution lookup latency and registration scaling are also unmeasured at that scale.

The adversarial evaluation supports narrower conclusions than the robustness discussion suggests. WEvade-B-Q achieves zero TDR/TAR, with image degradation measured afterward; this characterizes one attack’s quality trade-off rather than general black-box resistance. Targeted user impersonation, watermark transfer, and collusion deserve direct evaluation given the forensic motivation. Table 6 measures detection-level forgery on partly different watermarking systems and does not establish resistance to targeted false attribution.

Evaluation and reproducibility remain incomplete. Images are resized to 128×128, only 1,000 distinct test images per source are reused across users, and watermark insertion quality relative to the original images is not adequately quantified. Repeated-run uncertainty, detailed image-training configurations, and hardware information are missing, while release of the authors’ implementation and datasets is only promised.
